analysis.one_liner: Overrides state food safety warning labels with a single federal standard unless states win a federal exemption.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote, leaving state food warning laws untouched.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped states from setting their own food safety warning requirements — such as warnings on labels, posters, or in advertising — unless those warnings matched federal law exactly. States could have petitioned the federal government for an exemption or asked it to set a national standard, and could act on their own only for an imminent health hazard. The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: National food and beverage manufacturers benefit most: they would face one federal labeling and warning standard instead of a patchwork of stricter state rules, ending requirements like state-mandated safety warnings on labels, posters, or ads that differ from federal law ([S2], [S3]). States would get a petition route to ask the federal government for exemptions or national standards ([S2], [S3]).

how_it_helps.text: Gives national food and beverage manufacturers a single federal labeling and warning standard, ending the cost and complexity of meeting different state warning rules in different states

Lets a state petition the federal Secretary for an exemption for a rule protecting an important public interest, or to establish a national standard, with deadlines for the Secretary to act and court review if those deadlines are missed
Preserves state rules on freshness dating, open dating, grade labeling, organic or natural designations, unit pricing, and origin statements

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would pay by losing state-specific food warnings — any state safety warning that went beyond the federal label would be wiped out unless the state won a hard-to-get federal exemption ([S2], [S3]). State and local governments would pay by losing their power to set their own food safety and warning rules ([S2], [S3]).
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers relying on state food warnings

drawbacks.text: The bill would nullify state food safety warnings that go beyond federal law — covering warnings on labels, posters, public notices, and even advertising — so consumers in stricter states would stop seeing warnings they currently get

The state exemption process puts the decision entirely in the hands of the federal Secretary, who must weigh the state's public interest against the burden on interstate commerce, and a state cannot act on an imminent hazard without first filing a federal petition
Federal law sets no warning for many food hazards state laws cover, so 'uniformity' would in practice mean no warning at all in those cases

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: one national standard would cut labeling and compliance costs for food companies. The cost falls on consumers, who would lose state-level warnings — such as California's food hazard warnings — whenever federal law has no identical warning, and the exemption process is slow, discretionary, and weighted toward avoiding burdens on interstate commerce. The scales tip toward the industry that requested uniformity.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 27, 1998, by Senator Pat Roberts with nine cosponsors — six Republicans and three Democrats
It was referred to the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources the day it was introduced and the record shows no further action of any kind
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, without the committee acting, so state food warning laws were left untouched

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers who rely on state food safety warnings and the states that set them came out ahead, since the bill died without a vote and state warning authority remained intact. Food makers kept facing the existing patchwork of state rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and state warning laws survived

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — Senator Roberts was joined by six Republicans and three Democrats including Tom Harkin — but the bill was never voted on, so no party-line split appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have barred states from enforcing food safety warnings on labels, posters, or advertising unless they matched federal law exactly, eliminating stricter state requirements. That removes a compliance burden for multistate manufacturers but also removes warnings consumers would otherwise see.

industries.industry: State and local food safety regulators
industries.note: States and localities would lose the power to require safety warnings beyond the federal standard, keeping only a narrow imminent-hazard exception and a petition process for exemptions controlled by the federal Secretary.
Retailers selling in multiple states would benefit from one national label standard instead of carrying differently labeled or differently warned products for different states.
